title: C Extensions and pybind11
objectives: Decide when a compiled extension is justified, given profiling data and the alternatives ladder (algorithm fix, numpy, compile)
Read and write a minimal pybind11 module: PYBIND11_MODULE, m.def, build with a single c++ command
Explain the cost of pybind11 STL type conversions (copies) and use py::array_t to borrow numpy buffers without copying
Manage the GIL across long C++ calls with py::call_guard<py::gil_scoped_release> and state what becomes illegal after release
Choose among ctypes, the CPython C-API, Cython and pybind11 for a given integration problem
motivation: The profile is unambiguous: 90% of runtime sits in one pure-Python inner loop that numpy cannot express, a sequential order-book match or an online estimator. A 40-line C++ function bound with pybind11 can make it 50x faster while Python keeps doing orchestration. This lesson covers when dropping to C++ pays, how a binding actually works, and the traps, silent copies, the GIL, build pipelines, that turn a speed win into a maintenance sink.

blocks.text: When Python is the wrong material

blocks.md: NumPy vectorisation fixes elementwise loops; but some algorithms are inherently **sequential and stateful**, matching an order book tick by tick, updating an online covariance, walking a tree. They cannot be expressed as whole-array operations. The escalation ladder, in order: (1) fix the algorithm (the profiling lesson's heap example, usually the biggest win), (2) express it with numpy/scipy primitives, (3) compile it (Cython, pybind11, C-API), (4) parallelise across processes. Each rung costs build complexity and maintenance; a profile showing time concentrated in one pure-Python hot spot is the entry ticket for rung 3.

blocks.text: A pybind11 module end to end

blocks.md: pybind11 is a header-only C++ library that exposes C++ functions and classes as a Python extension module. You write the function, register it inside the `PYBIND11_MODULE` block, and compile to a `.so` that Python imports like any module. No boilerplate about reference counting, pybind11 manages it for you.

blocks.caption: fastmath.cpp, a sequential accumulation bound in a dozen lines.
One command builds the module; the suffix makes the filename importable on your interpreter (e.g. fastmath.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so).

blocks.code:
import fastmath
from functools import reduce

r = [0.1, -0.1, 0.05]
print(round(fastmath.compound(r), 4))                      # 1.0395
print(round(reduce(lambda v, x: v * (1 + x), r, 1.0), 4))  # 1.0395
blocks.caption: Same answer, different cost profile: the C++ loop runs compiled instructions; the reduce runs interpreted bytecodes. On large inputs the gap is 10-100x.

blocks.md: The binding has two hidden costs. First, **type conversion**: with `#include <pybind11/stl.h>`, the Python list argument is converted to a `std::vector<double>` by *copying* every element, an O(n) allocation per call. For a function called 10,000 times per second with 100k-element arrays, conversion can cost more than the maths. Second, the **GIL**: every pybind11 call holds the Global Interpreter Lock, so a 2-second C++ computation blocks every other Python thread. Release it for the duration of pure-C++ work:

blocks.caption: py::array_t borrows the buffer (no copy) and call_guard releases the GIL for the duration of the call, so other Python threads keep running.

blocks.md: The two-language stack is not an admission of weakness on either side, it is a deliberate division of labour. Python is where research lives: flexible, readable, immediate. C++ is where production lives: fast, deterministic, type-checked at compile time. The interop layer is where a quant shop's architecture is really decided, because whatever crosses the boundary pays a *crossing cost*, nanoseconds to microseconds per call, plus the cognitive cost of maintaining two type systems and two build systems.

blocks.caption: Interop is a funnel: keep the boundary narrow, marshal once, let the compiled side do the loop.

blocks.md: The performance law that governs all of this: **cross the boundary once per batch, never once per item**. A pybind11 call that receives a NumPy array, does all the work in C++, and returns one array, has effectively zero per-element overhead. The same functions exposed element-at-a-time (or called in a Python loop) pay the crossing cost n times and can end up slower than pure NumPy. When you profile a mixed Python/C++ system, the flame graph almost always shows the boundary as a fat bar, the fix is raising the granularity, not tuning the binding.

blocks.title: GIL, releases and object lifetimes
blocks.md: Three recurring failure modes: (1) pybind11 holds the GIL during your C++ by default, release it with `py::gil_scoped_release` for long computations or you serialise every Python thread waiting on you; (2) returning raw pointers to Python-managed memory is a lifetime bug, arrays own data, borrowed references do not; (3) exceptions must cross the boundary as Python exceptions (pybind11 translates automatically; hand-rolled C ABI does not and will segfault instead).

blocks.md: Three recurring failure modes: (1) pybind11 holds the GIL during your C++ by default, release it with `py::gil_scoped_release` for long computations or you serialise every Python thread waiting on you; (2) returning raw pointers to Python-managed memory is a lifetime bug, arrays own data, borrowed references do not; (3) exceptions must cross the boundary as Python exceptions (pybind11 translates automatically; hand-rolled C ABI does not and will segfault instead).

blocks.title: After gil_scoped_release, you are not allowed to touch Python
blocks.md: With the GIL released, any interaction with Python objects, printing via py::print, constructing py::object, raising pybind11 exceptions, races the interpreter and can crash it. If the C++ code must call back into Python, it must first re-acquire with `py::gil_scoped_acquire`. Keep released sections purely C++.

blocks.title: The desk pattern
blocks.md: A common production layout: Python owns strategy and I/O; C++ owns the tick-by-tick matching loop, invoked via a bound function taking a `py::array_t` of order updates and returning fills as numpy arrays, zero-copy in, zero-copy out, GIL released during matching. Python-side code stays auditable; the hot loop gets compiled speed.

Treat the binding as an untrusted reimplementation: unit-test it from Python against a reference implementation on identical inputs (including empty arrays, NaNs, single elements), and measure the speedup with the profiling lesson's harness. If the measured speedup is under ~2x, the build pipeline, version pinning and cross-platform compilation you just adopted are probably not worth it, ship the numpy version instead.

guidedExercise.prompt: Python calls `fastmath.compound([0.1, -0.1, 0.05])` (the stl.h version). Walk the call: (a) what happens to the list argument as it crosses into C++? (b) what runs inside C++? (c) what happens to the return value? (d) where is the O(n) cost, and how would you remove it if the input were a numpy array?
hints: stl.h converts between Python containers and C++ STL containers.
A Python float is itself a boxed object; a C++ double is raw.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) pybind11's stl conversion builds a `std::vector<double>` by copying each element out of the Python list, each element is unboxed from a PyObject float to a raw C double. (b) The compiled loop multiplies `(1 + x)` into `v` - machine-speed. (c) The returned double is boxed into a Python float object. (d) The O(n) argument copy. With numpy input, take `py::array_t<double>` and `request()` the buffer: the function reads the caller's memory directly, zero copy, and (as in the lesson) release the GIL while it runs.

independentExercise.prompt: Implement max drawdown as a pybind11 function `max_drawdown(const std::vector<double>& equity)`: single pass, maintain a running peak and the worst value of `equity[i]/peak - 1`. Write the C++ body, the `m.def` registration, the one-line build command, and verify against the numpy reference `(eq / np.maximum.accumulate(eq) - 1).min()` on `[100, 120, 90, 110]` (expected: -0.25). State the time and space complexity of your C++ version.
hints: Initialise peak with equity[0] and worst with 0.0 (drawdowns are <= 0).
One loop, two variables, no arrays allocated.
Compare floating-point results with a tolerance, not exact equality.

commonMistakes: Writing a C extension before profiling, binding the wrong 5% of the code buys nothing.
Passing big numpy arrays to functions taking std::vector via stl.h: every call silently copies the data; use py::array_t to borrow.
Doing long C++ computations while holding the GIL, all Python threads freeze; wrap with py::call_guard<py::gil_scoped_release>.
Touching Python objects (py::print, py::object) after releasing the GIL, undefined behaviour; re-acquire first.
Shipping bindings without differential tests against a Python reference, or without pinning the pybind11/compiler versions.
realWorldApplication: pandas, numpy and scikit-learn are themselves compiled extensions bound to Python; the same techniques scale down to a single hot function. Any Python system with a measured hot spot that numpy cannot express is a candidate for Cython/pybind11.
quantFinanceApplication: Trading systems commonly bind the order-book matching engine, options pricers or streaming risk kernels in C++ and keep the strategy layer in Python, pybind11 with array_t zero-copy buffers and GIL release around the tick loop is the standard recipe.
summary: Escalate performance work in order: algorithm fix, numpy/scipy, compiled extension, multiprocessing, and only enter rung 3 with a profile in hand.
A pybind11 module: include pybind11.h, write the function, register with m.def inside PYBIND11_MODULE, compile once with c++ -O3 -shared -std=c++17.
stl.h conversions copy Python containers into C++ containers (O(n) per call); py::array_t borrows a numpy buffer with zero copy.
Long pure-C++ calls should release the GIL (py::call_guard<py::gil_scoped_release>); while released, no Python API calls are legal.
Differential-test bindings against a Python reference and demand a measured >2x speedup before accepting the build complexity.

quiz.prompt: You need to call an existing C shared library from Python with the smallest possible build effort. Which tool fits best?
quiz.explanation: ctypes loads a compiled .so/.dll at runtime and calls it with hand-declared signatures, no compilation step of your own. Cython and pybind11 need a build; the C-API is maximal boilerplate.

quiz.code:
from functools import reduce
r = [0.1, -0.1, 0.05]
print(round(reduce(lambda v, x: v * (1 + x), r, 1.0), 4))
quiz.explanation: Compounding: $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$, then $0.99 \times 1.05 = 1.0395$. This is the reference implementation the C++ binding must match exactly.

quiz.prompt: A pybind11 function declared to take `std::vector<double>` (with stl.h) receives a 1,000,000-element Python list on every call. What is the main per-call cost?
options: An O(n) copy that converts every element from a boxed PyObject float to a raw C double
Nothing, std::vector borrows the list's memory
A JIT compilation of the loop
quiz.explanation: stl.h performs a value conversion: it allocates a vector and copies/converts each element. For large arrays called often, use py::array_t to borrow the numpy buffer with zero copy.

quiz.prompt: Which are good reasons NOT to write a C++ extension? Select all that apply.
options: The hot loop can already be expressed as a couple of numpy whole-array operations
The measured speedup of the prototype binding is only 1.5x
The algorithm is inherently sequential and numpy cannot express it
The team has no experience maintaining compiled C++ build pipelines
quiz.explanation: numpy already gives compiled speed for vectorisable work; sub-2x speedups rarely justify build complexity and version pinning; maintenance capability matters. The one legitimate trigger, a sequential numpy-inexpressible hot spot, is deliberately NOT a reason to skip.

quiz.prompt: What does py::call_guard<py::gil_scoped_release>() on an m.def registration do?
options: Makes the function release the GIL for the duration of the call, letting other Python threads run
Disables the GIL permanently while the module is loaded
Pickles the arguments so the call can run in a subprocess
Converts the function to a coroutine
quiz.explanation: The guard releases the Global Interpreter Lock on entry and re-acquires it on exit, so a long C++ computation no longer blocks every other Python thread. While released, the code must not touch the Python API.

quiz.prompt: How many bytes does a numpy array of 1,000,000 float64 elements occupy for its data (header aside)?
quiz.explanation: float64 = 8 bytes per element, contiguous: $10^6 \times 8 = 8{,}000{,}000$ bytes. Compare with a Python list of a million boxed floats: ~8 MB of pointers + ~24 MB of float objects.

flashcards.back: Header-only C++ library that exposes C++ functions/classes as Python extension modules: PYBIND11_MODULE + m.def, compiled with c++ -O3 -shared -std=c++17 into an importable .so.
stl.h converts Python list <-> std::vector by copying every element (O(n) per call). py::array_t<double> + request() borrows the numpy buffer with zero copy, the choice for large arrays.

flashcards.front: Spot the bug: m.def("f", &f, py::call_guard<py::gil_scoped_release>()); and f calls py::print(...) mid-computation
flashcards.back: With the GIL released, touching Python objects races the interpreter, crashes or corruption. Re-acquire with py::gil_scoped_acquire before any Python API call, or keep the released section pure C++.
1.04, precisely 1.0395: (1.1)(0.9)(1.05). The binding must match a Python reference implementation exactly.

flashcards.front: The escalation ladder before binding C++
flashcards.back: 1) Fix the algorithm. 2) numpy/scipy primitives. 3) Compile (Cython/pybind11/C-API). 4) Multiprocessing. A profile with time concentrated in one pure-Python hot spot is the ticket to step 3.
